text.p: President Fidel Ramos signed a law on Wednesday strengthening the Philippines' anti-corruption court, enabling it to widen its scope in prosecuting senior officials involved in graft.
"Today, we take a giant stride in our crusade against graft and corruption," Ramos said, stressing the new law would enhance the effectiveness of the special court in curbing misdeeds in government.
Officials say the Philippines has lost $48 billion in the past 20 years to corruption, with most of the money being laundered and hidden in foreign banks, foundations and investment houses.
The anti-graft court, called the Sandiganbayan, exclusively tries cases against officials charged with corruption.

The old law, however, allows it to try senior officials only if they are the main or principal defendants in a case. The new law widens the court's powers to try senior officials even if they are charged only as accomplices, such as those accused of covering up a crime.
To enable the court to dispose of thousands of pending cases, many of which involve low-level officials, the new law establishes a salary grade level for cases that may be brought before it.
All cases involving officials or employees below that level are to be tried by regular courts, it said.
Ramos said last month corruption in the government had become a "nightmare".

He said the people had become so sceptical that accusations of corruption were accepted as fact not because the charges were credible "but because graft in the government has become accepted as a commonplace malady".
